title: What chemistry studies
description: Chemistry is the study of matter: what it is made of (composition), how it looks and behaves (properties) and how it changes when it meets other matter (interactions).

facts.text: Chemistry is the study of the composition, properties and interactions of matter: what things are made of and how they change.
A substance's properties include how it looks and behaves, such as its hardness and whether it burns (flammability).

title: Chemistry began in kitchens and workshops
description: People practiced chemistry long before it was a science: controlling fire to cook, fire pottery and smelt metals, and fermenting food and drink.

facts.text: Humans began to practice chemistry when they learned to control fire and use it to cook, make pottery and smelt metals; cooking, fermentation, glass making and metalworking date from the beginnings of civilization.

title: Chemistry, the central science
description: Chemistry is called the central science because it connects to so many other fields, from biology (through biochemistry) to medicine, materials and the environment.

facts.text: Chemistry is sometimes called "the central science" because it connects with many other fields, such as biology, medicine, materials science, forensics and environmental science.
Chemistry and biology meet in biochemistry, the study of the substances in living things and how they change.
Digesting food, making the polymers used in clothing and credit cards, and refining crude oil into gasoline are all examples of chemistry.

title: What counts as matter
description: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space: an ant, a truck, a galaxy, and invisible air too.

facts.text: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space (occupies volume), from an ant to a truck to a whole galaxy.
Gases are matter too: if gases did not take up space, a balloon would not get bigger when filled with gas.
Dry air has a density of about 1.2 grams per liter, so the 50,000 liters of air in a room 4 m by 5 m with a 2.5 m ceiling has a mass of about 60 kilograms.

title: Mass is not weight
description: Mass is the amount of matter in something; weight is the pull of gravity on it. On the Moon an astronaut weighs one-sixth as much but has the same mass.

facts.text: Mass is the amount of matter in an object; weight is the pull of gravity on it. On the Moon, whose gravity is one-sixth of Earth's, an astronaut has the same mass but one-sixth the weight.

title: Solid, liquid and gas
description: A solid is rigid with a definite shape and volume; a liquid flows and takes its container's shape but keeps its volume; a gas takes both the shape and volume of its container.

facts.text: A solid is rigid with a definite shape and volume; a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container but keeps its volume; a gas takes both the shape and the volume of its container.

title: Particles explain the states
description: Matter is made of tiny particles. In a solid they are packed tight and vibrate in place; in a liquid they are close but slide past each other; in a gas they are far apart and move freely.

facts.text: All matter is made of tiny particles: atoms, which can join into molecules.

In a solid, particles are tightly packed, often in a regular pattern, and vibrate about fixed positions; in a liquid they stay close but move past each other; in a gas they are far apart and move independently except when they collide.

title: What melting and boiling do to particles
description: Heating gives particles more energy. Enough energy frees them from fixed places (melting) or from their neighbors entirely (boiling). While a substance changes state, its temperature holds steady.

facts.text: Heating raises the kinetic energy of particles, so they move faster; with enough energy they overcome the attractions holding them, and the substance melts or boils.
While a substance is changing state, such as ice melting or water boiling, its temperature stays constant: the heat goes into pulling particles apart rather than speeding them up.
Ice, liquid water and steam are the same substance, water, in different states.

title: Boiling points depend on pressure
description: Water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at sea-level pressure. Boiling happens when the vapor pushes back as hard as the air pressing down, so with less air pressure (up a mountain) water boils cooler, about 90 °C in Leadville, Colorado.

facts.text: Ice melts at 0 °C, and water boils at 100 °C at sea-level air pressure (1 atmosphere).
A liquid boils when its vapor pushes out as hard as the surrounding pressure pushes in, so lower air pressure means a lower boiling point.
In Leadville, Colorado, about 10,200 feet (3,100 m) up in the Rocky Mountains, water boils at about 90 °C, about 10 °C below its sea-level boiling point.
Melting points shift with pressure too, but far less: water's melting point drops only slightly as pressure rises.

title: Plasma, the fourth state
description: Plasma is a gas so energized that electrons are torn from its atoms, leaving a mix of electrically charged particles that conducts electricity. Heat or high voltage, like lightning, makes it.

facts.text: Plasma, a fourth state of matter, is a gas containing many electrically charged particles; it forms when electrons (tiny charged particles from inside atoms) are torn free from gas atoms, for example by intense heat, and it conducts electricity.
Lightning turns the air in its path into plasma; high-voltage electricity can tear electrons free.
Lightning can heat the air in its channel to about 50,000 °F, about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.

title: Plasma fills the universe
description: The Sun and other stars are mostly plasma, so nearly all the visible matter in the universe is plasma, even though on Earth we meet it mainly in lightning and auroras.

facts.text: Nearly all the visible matter in the universe is plasma, because the Sun and other stars are mostly plasma; this counts ordinary matter, not dark matter.
On Earth, natural plasma appears in lightning and in the aurora, the glowing curtains of light near the poles.

title: Mixtures and pure substances
description: A mixture is two or more kinds of matter mingled in amounts that can vary, and it can be separated by physical means. A heterogeneous mixture, like a chocolate chip cookie, is not the same all the way through.

facts.text: A mixture is two or more kinds of matter mingled in amounts that can vary, and it can be separated by physical means; a pure substance always has the same composition.
A heterogeneous mixture is not the same all the way through; chocolate chip cookies, granite and Italian salad dressing are examples.

title: Solutions
description: A solution is a homogeneous mixture, the same all the way through. The dissolved substance is the solute and the one doing the dissolving is the solvent. Solutions can be liquids, gases (air) or solids (brass).

facts.text: A homogeneous mixture, the same all the way through, is called a solution; salt water, maple syrup, gasoline and air are examples.
In a solution, the substance that gets dissolved is the solute and the one doing the dissolving is usually called the solvent; you can add more solute only up to a limit, its solubility.
Solutions need not be liquid: air is a solution of mostly nitrogen and oxygen, and brass is a solid solution of copper and zinc.

title: Filtering and evaporating
description: Mixtures are separated by physical differences. A filter holds back solid bits like sand but lets dissolved salt through with the water; evaporating the water then leaves the salt behind.

facts.text: Mixtures can be separated by physical methods such as filtration, evaporation and distillation, which use differences in the parts' physical properties.
Filtration removes solid particles from a liquid or gas using a filter that lets the fluid through but holds back the solids, as when brewing coffee.
In a sand, salt and water mixture, the sand stays behind as a solid while the dissolved salt goes along with the water, so filtering alone cannot remove the salt.
Evaporating the water from a salt solution leaves the salt behind; in many parts of the world, table salt is obtained by evaporating seawater.

title: Distillation
description: Distillation heats a liquid to vapor and cools the vapor back to liquid somewhere else. Because parts of a mixture turn to vapor at different temperatures, it can make fresh water from seawater.

facts.text: Distillation turns a liquid into vapor and then condenses the vapor back into liquid; because the parts of a mixture boil at different temperatures, the lowest-boiling part comes off first.
Distillation can produce fresh water from seawater, leaving the salt behind.
More than 2,300 years ago, Aristotle (384 to 322 BCE) noted that evaporating seawater makes pure water.

title: Density
description: Density is mass divided by volume: how much mass is packed into each bit of space. Water is about 1 gram per cubic centimeter.

facts.text: Density is an object's mass divided by its volume: how much mass is packed into a given space, so equal masses can take up very different volumes.
Liquid water has a density of about 1 gram per cubic centimeter.

title: Float or sink
description: An object floats if its average density is less than the liquid's and sinks if it is denser. Weight alone does not decide it: a big log floats while a small iron nail sinks.

facts.text: An object floats if its average density is less than that of the liquid around it and sinks if it is denser.
Wood floats on water because it is less dense than water, while iron sinks because it is denser.
The fraction of a floating object that sits below the surface equals its density compared with the liquid's, so ice, only a little less dense than water, floats mostly submerged.

title: Why ice floats
description: Frozen water molecules lock into an open, spread-out pattern, so ice is only about 90 percent as dense as liquid water, and it floats. Salty seawater is denser still.

facts.text: Ice is less dense than liquid water, about 90 percent as dense (about 0.92 versus 1.0 grams per cubic centimeter), which is why ice floats.
When water freezes, its molecules lock into an open lattice that spreads them farther apart than in the liquid; water is unusual in this.
Dissolved salt makes seawater denser than pure water.

title: Physical change
description: In a physical change, matter changes form or state but stays the same substance: melting, boiling, tearing, grinding. Boiling water bubbles, but it is still water.

facts.text: In a physical change, matter changes its form or state but not its identity; melting wax or ice, boiling water, tearing paper and grinding a solid into powder are physical changes.
Clues to a chemical change include an unexpected color change, a new smell, heat or light given off, and gas bubbles; but boiling also makes bubbles without making any new substance.

title: Chemical change
description: In a chemical change at least one new substance forms: rusting, burning, cooking meat, a banana browning. Chemical changes are often harder to undo.

facts.text: In a chemical change at least one new substance forms; iron rusting, a match or candle burning, meat cooking and a banana browning are chemical changes.
When a candle burns, the wax reacts to form new substances, carbon dioxide and water.
Chemical changes are often harder to reverse than physical ones.

title: Gray areas between the two kinds of change
description: The line between physical and chemical change is not perfectly sharp. Dissolving salt is usually called physical, yet some chemists argue otherwise; and reversibility is no sure test, since a rechargeable battery reverses a chemical change.

facts.text: The distinction between physical and chemical change is not clear cut; some science educators describe it as more of a continuum, and salt dissolving in water is a debated case.
Salt dissolving in water is usually classified as a physical change, though the dissolved salt comes apart into charged particles in the water.
Reversibility is not a reliable test: a rechargeable battery reverses a chemical change each time it is charged.

title: Sublimation and deposition
description: Some solids turn straight into gas (sublimation): dry ice at normal pressure, and snow slowly even below freezing. The reverse, gas straight to solid, is deposition, as in frost. Both are physical changes.

facts.text: Sublimation is a solid turning straight into a gas; dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) sublimes at normal air pressure instead of melting, and snow and ice slowly sublime below freezing, faster in wind and the low pressure of high altitudes.
Deposition is the reverse of sublimation, a gas turning straight into a solid; frost forming is an example.
